outcome: No source I read establishes that every group is surjunctive or that some group is not; the only claimed full resolution (Cannizzo, arXiv:1912.00541, 2019) was withdrawn by its author, and the 2025-2026 literature still calls the problem open. The one 2026 event bearing on it, OpenAI's claimed explicit non-sofic group (announced 1 Aug 2026, attributed to an internal version of the forthcoming Astra model), concerns soficity, not surjunctivity: if accepted it shows not every group is sofic, but per the OpenAI chapter as reproduced by a secondary source the surjunctivity of that group is listed as open.
problem_asks: One question with its quantifiers unpacked. (a) For every group G, with no restriction to finitely generated, sofic, amenable or residually finite groups. (b) For every finite alphabet A (equivalently every finite set Sigma, Gottschalk's formulation). (c) Every continuous, G-equivariant, injective map A^G to A^G (a cellular automaton) is surjective. Equivalently, in Gottschalk's terms: no group admits a continuous G-equivariant injective non-surjective self-map of a full shift over a finite alphabet, i.e. no strict self-embedding of the shift. The statement asks a yes/no question about all groups; it names no subclass.

events.what_happened: Mikhail Gromov, 'Endomorphisms of symbolic algebraic varieties' (IHES preprint M/98/56, July 1998; J. Eur. Math. Soc. 1 (1999), 109-197). Secondary sources credit Gromov with the result that cellular automata over sofic groups are surjunctive, and with implicitly introducing the sofic notion; Weiss later named it (event weiss-2000). I did not open the preprint or the journal article. The one abstract excerpt I saw states surjunctivity for proregular maps of proalgebraic varieties commuting with sufficiently large automorphism groups; I could not map that statement onto the sofic-group theorem.
events.revisions: IHES preprint M/98/56 (July 1998); journal version J. Eur. Math. Soc. 1 (1999), no. 2, 109-197, DOI 10.1007/PL00011162 (received Aug 1998, final Jan 1999 per the abstract page excerpt).
events.delivers: Per secondary citations: every sofic group is surjunctive. Restriction: sofic groups only, which are all residually finite and all amenable groups (per secondary sources). The exact theorem covering sofic groups in the preprint was not confirmed by me.
events.remains: Every group that is not sofic. Whether every group is sofic was open at the time; the Astra claim (event openai-astra-2026-08-01), if accepted, answers it negatively.

events.what_happened: Jan Cannizzo, 'All groups are surjunctive', arXiv:1912.00541. The v1 abstract claims that for any finitely generated group G and any k >= 1, the space of k-colourings of G admits no strict self-embedding, and says this 'settles the Gottschalk surjunctivity conjecture and, consequently, Kaplansky's direct finiteness conjecture'. The v2 withdrawal comment says that 'several people have pointed out' that 'the last sentence of Lemma 5.3 is not justified', that this 'likely counts as a fatal flaw that invalidates the main theorem (Theorem 5.4)', and that the author 'hereby retract[s] the claimed result'. I read the abstract page and version history. The PDF returned HTTP 404 to my fetch, so the argument itself is unread.

events.delivers: As claimed in v1: the full conjecture for finitely generated groups (the abstract's statement). The abstract does not say how arbitrary groups are reached. Retracted by the author, so nothing is established by this event.

events.what_happened: OpenAI's post 'Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science' (1 Aug 2026) includes a result that the unit group of the binary Leavitt algebra L_F2(1,2) over the two-element field is not sofic. It is reported as the first explicit construction of a non-sofic group and as a counterexample to the soficity conjecture. A 249-page manuscript collection and Lean 4 formalisations (github.com/openai/ten-proofs, file NonSoficGroup.lean) were released. Coverage says an internal version of the forthcoming Astra model produced the arguments. The openai.com page returned HTTP 403 to my fetch in both locales, so the chapter text was read through a secondary reproduction (blog.ecitis.org, dated 4 Aug 2026) and the Rényi Institute news item (4 Aug 2026). Secondary reports say a document titled 'Nonsofic Groups Exist' circulated on X on 31 Jul 2026, before the official release.
events.revisions: A 'Nonsofic Groups Exist' document circulated on X on 31 Jul 2026 (secondary reports); official post 1 Aug 2026. Per Scientific American (6 Aug 2026), OpenAI revised the 'no progress for a decade' wording and planned 'small updates' to the paper. Per aiweekly (search result), OpenAI revised the writeup to credit Thom and Kun; not checked at source. Date recorded as 1 Aug because the official post is the first public release I can pin to a source; the 31 Jul circulation is the alternative.
events.delivers: If accepted: at least one countable group, the unit group of L_F2(1,2), is not sofic. Restriction: this is a soficity result. It establishes nothing about whether any group is surjunctive. Non-sofic does not imply non-surjunctive. Per the chapter text (secondary reproduction), the surjunctivity of this group is listed as open, and the chapter says that if the group were not surjunctive, Gottschalk's conjecture would be false. Gromov and Weiss make sofic groups surjunctive, so this group falls outside the one class where surjunctivity was already known; no known result gives its surjunctivity either way.
events.remains: Whether every group is surjunctive, including whether this group is surjunctive (listed as open per the chapter text). Whether every group is sofic is answered negatively if the claim is accepted, which bears on the Gromov-Weiss route, not on the question itself.

events.object: The unit group of the binary Leavitt algebra L_F2(1,2) over the two-element field: a countable group. The claim is that it is not sofic, so finite permutation approximations of its multiplication table do not exist. Per the chapter reproduced by blog.ecitis.org and the Rényi report, the proof passes to a finitely generated subgroup with property (T) containing a copy of Thompson's group V, and uses Kun's expander decomposition and the Kun-Thom centralizer theorem to derive a contradiction. events.what_happened: Two manuscripts claim a negative answer, each by exhibiting a group with an injective, non-surjective cellular automaton over a finite field. (1) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two': for a finite field K of characteristic two, a finitely presented group G containing an element of odd prime order, and sums a, b in K[G] with ab=1 and ba≠1 (Theorem 1.1). The coefficients of b give a local rule with memory supp(b). The map Tᵦ: K^G→K^G on all configurations is injective, because a is a left inverse, and not surjective, because a point indicator δₕ with (ba−1)ₕ≠0 has no preimage. Its corollary on non-surjunctivity states that G is not surjunctive. Its F∞ corollary also gives an overgroup U with the same failure, conditional on an external embedding theorem. (2) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Odd Characteristic': for p the least prime divisor of (m!)²+1 with m = binom(1200,600), an odd prime, a field K of order p⁴, a finitely generated group G with torsion, and sums a, b in K[G] with ab=1 and ba≠1. Its Section 06 applies the same transfer to these sums, giving an injective, non-surjective cellular automaton on K^G, and states that this negatively answers Gottschalk's surjunctivity conjecture. 'A Torsion-Free Group Algebra That Is Not Directly Finite' and 'A Counterexample to the Group-Ring Determinant Conjecture' do not treat cellular automata.
events.delivers: If the claims hold, they answer the list's question negatively. The question asks whether every group is surjunctive, for every finite alphabet, with every injective cellular automaton surjective. One group, one finite alphabet and one injective non-surjective automaton refute that, and each of (1) and (2) supplies one. Restrictions: each gives a single group. Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture asserts that $ab=1$ implies $ba=1$ for $a,b\in K[G]$, for every field $K$ and group $G$. The formalized results construct a finite field of characteristic two and a group algebra violating this implication. One statement records the counterexample for a finitely generated group; the more detailed construction gives a finitely presented group with an element of odd prime order.

The detailed construction also gives a precise recipe for choosing the data and proves that the required search terminates. The further conclusion that the group is nonsofic is outside these statements.

A nonsingular integer matrix has absolute determinant at least $1$. The group-ring Determinant Conjecture extends this bound to matrices over $\mathbb Z[G]$ for every discrete group $G$. If $T_A$ is the operator induced by such a matrix $A$ on finite direct sums of $\ell^2(G)$, and $\mu_A$ is the spectral measure of $T_A^*T_A$ with respect to the group trace, the conjecture asserts

$\displaystyle \int_{(0,\infty)}\log t\,d\mu_A(t)\ge0,$

with the zero spectral atom omitted. For an invertible square matrix, this is equivalent to its Fuglede–Kadison determinant being at least $1$.

The formalized result contradicts that bound. It gives a finitely generated group $G$ and an $n\times n$ matrix over $\mathbb Z[G]$, with $n\ge1$, that is invertible over $\mathbb Q[G]$. Its bounded left-regular operator is invertible and has determinant strictly between $0$ and $1$.

The formalization uses the trace of $\log(T^*T)$ to define the determinant for the invertible operator $T$. The paper's additional spectral-measure integral conclusion is not included.

disputes.summary: Andreas Thom (TU Dresden) says the key step of OpenAI's non-sofic proof rests on his 2019 joint work with Gábor Kun, and that he spent months discussing the same mathematics with ChatGPT before the announcement. He asked OpenAI whether those conversations entered training data or were accessible while the model worked. OpenAI's Mark Sellke replied 'Regarding your conversations with ChatGPT: that did not happen' (as Thom published it), which Thom calls evasive. OpenAI says it did not access chats directly but cannot rule out de-identified data (secondary coverage). Bubeck is reported as saying 'We did not use their prompt or proofs to prompt our models' (secondary coverage). No independent evidence that anything was taken was found. Claim unverified.

OpenAI's first writeup did not credit Kun and Thom; secondary coverage reports OpenAI updated it to credit them after mathematicians noticed. The Rényi Institute says the manuscript itself identifies Kun's decomposition theorem and the Kun-Thom result as its principal inputs. Kun and Thom describe their follow-up as building on OpenAI's breakthrough.
OpenAI's first announcement described the ten problems as having seen no progress for at least a decade. Scientific American's experts dispute this, and OpenAI has revised the wording (6 Aug 2026).

Fournier-Facio says the non-sofic result assembled existing ideas and was not as novel as it first appeared (Scientific American). Gowers reads it as a first example rather than a counterexample (17 Aug 2026 article). Secondary reports attribute to Gowers a remark that he would recommend the proof for Annals of Mathematics; the article I read contains no such remark, so the Annals claim is unconfirmed.

summary: I ran 44 web searches and opened 24 URLs (several PDF bodies did not decode, so those were read as metadata only). The question as worded is open in every source I read, as of the latest source I found (11 Sep 2026). Old results: Gromov (1998/99) and Weiss (2000) show sofic groups are surjunctive; residually finite (Lawton, or Lawson) and amenable (Garden of Eden) groups are known to be surjunctive. The only claimed full resolution I found, Cannizzo's arXiv:1912.00541 (2019), was withdrawn in v2 on 4 Dec 2019 by its author, who retracts the result because the final sentence of Lemma 5.3 is unjustified; I read this on the abstract page but could not open the PDF (404). Several AI and aggregator search summaries present Cannizzo as an unverified live claim; the arXiv record I read shows it withdrawn. In the window (Jan 2024 to Oct 2026), the surjunctivity papers are conditional or about neighbouring objects: Ceccherini-Silberstein-Coornaert-Phung (2023, published 2025; 2024 monoids), Phung (2025 NUCA; 2026 post-injunctive, which says the group question is not known), Bowen-Chapman (Nov 2025, surjunctive IRS that is not cosofic; the group-level question is stated open), and Ersoy (Apr 2026, conditional on non-sofic groups existing). The one event bearing on this problem with an AI system involved is OpenAI's 1 Aug 2026 announcement: the unit group of the binary Leavitt algebra over F2 is not sofic, attributed to an internal version of the forthcoming Astra model. Whether it bears on the problem at all is a close call. Gromov-Weiss make sofic groups surjunctive, so a non-sofic group removes the class where this group's surjunctivity was known; it neither settles nor refutes surjunctivity for that group, and the chapter text (read via a secondary reproduction, since openai.com returned 403) says its surjunctivity is open. I recorded it as an event with its AI involvement, and flagged the adjacency in delivers and remains. The 'Astra' system entry rests on a third-party quotation of OpenAI's post, not the post itself, and the only other AI-attribution text I have from OpenAI is a spokesperson's 'We take responsibility for the correctness of these results', which says nothing about what the model did. The leak-stage name 'GPT 5.6 Sol' appears only in secondary headlines, so I did not record it as a separate system. Date call: the official release is 1 Aug 2026, but a 'Nonsofic Groups Exist' document circulated on X on 31 Jul per secondary reports; the later pass should choose. The mathematical attribution is disputed: Thom says the key step uses his and Kun's 2019 work and that his ChatGPT sessions were involved; OpenAI denies direct access. Experts (Fournier-Facio; Scientific American) say the result assembles existing ideas rather than making a leap, and Gowers reads it as a first example rather than a counterexample. The record has no journal acceptance and no independent replication. The Navier-Stokes and sphere-packing claims from the same OpenAI batch concern other problems and are not recorded.
competing_reading: (a) The non-sofic group is the strongest candidate so far for a non-surjunctive group, because several experts believe Gottschalk's conjecture is false (Bowen-Chapman; a secondary summary). On that reading the event bears on this problem directly, not as an adjacent soficity result. Against: non-sofic does not imply non-surjunctive, and nobody has shown this group fails to be surjunctive. (b) Cannizzo 2019 could be read as a claimed full resolution dated 2019. Against: the v2 withdrawal retracts it, so it establishes nothing. (c) On the AI question, a reader could treat the model as a tool that reproduced a human's unpublished route (Thom's reading), so that the model's contribution is not load-bearing. OpenAI's account is that the model generated the arguments, which would make it load-bearing. The record leaves that call to the later pass.
what_would_settle_it: (1) OpenAI's manuscript and Lean development, read by group theorists: whether the formal definitions match the intended Leavitt algebra, unit group and soficity, and whether the proof is sorry-free. (2) A refereed publication of the non-sofic result, and whether its statement and proof survive review. (3) A determination of whether the non-sofic group (or any known non-sofic group) is surjunctive, or a proof that some group is not. (4) The full text of Cannizzo v1 and any corrigendum, to confirm the gap identified in v2. (5) The full texts of Bowen-Chapman, Phung 2026 and Kun-Thom: their reference lists (whether later work cites Cannizzo), their acknowledgements (AI disclosure), and their introductions. (6) OpenAI's manuscript author list, and a response to Thom's allegation and to the Scientific American experts. (7) Thom's Mastodon posts and any further OpenAI statement on training data.

event.what_happened: Two manuscripts claim a negative answer, each by exhibiting a group with an injective, non-surjective cellular automaton over a finite field. (1) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two': for a finite field K of characteristic two, a finitely presented group G containing an element of odd prime order, and sums a, b in K[G] with ab=1 and ba≠1 (Theorem 1.1). The coefficients of b give a local rule with memory supp(b). The map Tᵦ: K^G→K^G on all configurations is injective, because a is a left inverse, and not surjective, because a point indicator δₕ with (ba−1)ₕ≠0 has no preimage. Its corollary on non-surjunctivity states that G is not surjunctive. Its F∞ corollary also gives an overgroup U with the same failure, conditional on an external embedding theorem. (2) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Odd Characteristic': for p the least prime divisor of (m!)²+1 with m = binom(1200,600), an odd prime, a field K of order p⁴, a finitely generated group G with torsion, and sums a, b in K[G] with ab=1 and ba≠1. Its Section 06 applies the same transfer to these sums, giving an injective, non-surjective cellular automaton on K^G, and states that this negatively answers Gottschalk's surjunctivity conjecture. 'A Torsion-Free Group Algebra That Is Not Directly Finite' and 'A Counterexample to the Group-Ring Determinant Conjecture' do not treat cellular automata.

judgement.why: The statement is a single universal yes/no over all groups, so one group with an injective non-surjective cellular automaton over a finite alphabet answers it in full. openai-math-197 claims exactly that: a group algebra K[G] over a finite field with ab=1, ba≠1, and the standard transfer (b gives an injective CA on K^G, not surjective since ba≠1) — consistent with the published fact that surjunctive groups have stably finite group rings (ceccherini-2023). So it is scope whole, direction refuted, object a counterexample; it is unreviewed (8 days old, only a Lean build with sorry status unknown and no human reader). I kept it credible: there is no specific error, and the non-executed search prescription is a termination/existence argument, not a gap; but it is a landmark claim resting only on machine checking. AI role generated, from the repository's statement that results were obtained by the internal model. The Astra non-sofic result and its human follow-ups (Fournier-Facio, Kun-Thom) concern soficity, not surjunctivity — non-sofic does not imply non-surjunctive and the chapter lists this group's surjunctivity as open — so they are variants; Bowen-Chapman (IRSs) and the 2024 monoid paper likewise. Pre-snapshot class results (sofic, residually finite, amenable) are cases; the undated Lawton and amenable entries are placed before the snapshot because the record cites them in a 2010 book. Cannizzo and Shahryari are withdrawn.
judgement.doubts: openai-math-197 is 8 days old with no human engagement; the README quote is a blanket statement about 'the vast majority of results' rather than this result specifically, and no individual human authors are named. The Lean scope covers the direct-finiteness counterexamples and, for the odd-characteristic case, states the CA is injective but not surjective; whether its definitions match the standard ones was not audited. A Kaplansky direct-finiteness counterexample would itself imply a non-sofic group, so this claim is consistent with the Astra event but makes a much stronger assertion; readers should treat it as a claimed refutation pending expert review.
